Novig Sues Ohio Regulators Over Sports Event Contracts

Published November 18, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Novig, a sports event-contracts platform, filed a federal complaint against officials of the Ohio Casino Control Commission on Monday, November 16, seeking an injunction to stop the state from enforcing its sports gambling law against Novig's products. It's the latest filing in a widening legal fight between prediction-market operators and state gaming regulators that has already produced conflicting rulings in multiple federal circuits this year.

What Novig is arguing

Novig's complaint contends that its sports-based event contracts are swaps — listed, traded, and settled on federally registered derivatives exchanges — and are therefore regulated exclusively at the federal level, outside the reach of Ohio's state gambling statutes. That's the same core preemption argument prediction-market operators including Kalshi have made in parallel lawsuits against other states this year, with mixed results depending on the court.

Part of Ohio's broader crackdown

The lawsuit follows cease-and-desist notices Ohio's gaming regulator sent in October to ten prediction-market companies, with Novig among the firms named. Ohio has been one of the more aggressive states in pushing back against sports-related event contracts, arguing they function as unlicensed sports betting regardless of how they're structured or labeled on a federally registered exchange.

The dispute sits inside a larger, unresolved legal question playing out across several federal circuits at once: whether the Commodity Exchange Act preempts state gambling law when it comes to sports event contracts, or whether states retain authority to regulate anything that functions like sports betting no matter which federal exchange lists it. Courts have split on that question depending on the jurisdiction, and Ohio's case adds one more data point to a conflict that increasingly looks headed for appellate — or eventually Supreme Court — resolution.

Why it matters to a US bettor

For bettors and casual users of prediction-market apps, the practical stakes are about product availability rather than anything that affects an existing wager: if Ohio successfully enforces its cease-and-desist order, Novig's sports-based contracts could become unavailable to Ohio residents, similar to restrictions already in place in other states that have taken action against event-contract platforms. The case is also a reminder that prediction markets, however they're marketed, remain in a genuinely unsettled legal position in much of the country — a materially different footing than a licensed, regulated sportsbook operating under a state's actual gaming law.
